newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ short end bathes in post-coalition sunshine.
newsitem.headline: NZ short end bathes in post-coalition sunshine.

text.p: New Zealand money markets added another 10 basis points during Wednesday's session to the gains made at the open, rallying almost half a percentage point by the close.

Sentiment in the short end was buoyant as the market revelled in the return to power of the caretaker conservative National Party, in the form of a coalition deal with nationalist NZ First. The news was announced after the local Tuesday close.

The long bond did not fare so well on the day, ending eight points lower in yield at 7.20 percent after a rally at the open of 17 basis points. Dealers said the 11/06 maturity had hit a wall of resistance around 7.10 percent.
"I guess the flows we saw were probably net selling, and there is a general acceptance that the most likely scenario is that the bond curve will go more positive," one bond dealer said.

"The long end was always under pressure -- you're talking about a higher inflation target, higher spending. You can assume confidence levels will pick up, which will flow through to activity," he said.
The new coalition government has widened the target band for underlying inflation to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent, and outlined planned rises in government spending.

Dealers saw potential for further falls in short rates in the near term. They suggested there was also further downside in the two to five year part of the curve, especially after a 50 basis point cut in Australia's official interest rates to 6.0 percent.

New Zealand five year rates were still very attractive to offshore investors, and the Australian easing made them even One Wellington dealer said the extent of the positive steepening of the yield curve would depend on flows and on traders' perceptions of where New Zealand should settle on the spreads to dollar bloc markets.

"We're back out to 100 over (U.S.) Treasuries, and some people think it should be 50 over. Some think should be in line with where Australia is trading," he said, adding that offshore holders were the major investors in New Zealand and would have the final say.

"Some may decide it's worth buying because it's a small market and it's easy to squeeze the margin in, and others may just sell into it. I get the impression there are probably people waiting to sell rather than buy," the dealer said.
